rows: An owl's eyes face forward, so their views overlap across about 45 degrees in front, more than in most birds. Its whole view spans about 200 degrees.
An owl's eyes barely move in their sockets, by less than one degree, so the owl turns its whole head to look, as far as about 270 degrees.

A barn owl sees only a fifteenth to a twentieth as much detail as a person does, and other owls measured average about a third. This view is blurred to about a sixth of a person's sharpness, between the two.
A tawny owl's eye works close to the limit that any vertebrate eye can reach in dim light. This view brightens the shadows.
Owls have lost the colour-sensing cells for violet and ultraviolet light that other birds have, and only about one cone in ten carries a coloured droplet of oil. This view mutes colours.
Owls can find and catch prey by sound alone. A barn owl hears faint sounds about 20 decibels quieter than other birds can, and hears pitches above 10,000 vibrations a second.

With the microphone on, the picture rests dark and each sound lights it for a moment, high sounds most. How an owl's hearing feels is unknown, and the drawing is the app's. Where the phone can vibrate it can also buzz with each sound (&draw=buzz).
The pupil, the depth of focus, the trails and how fast sharpness falls from the centre are the app's guesses.
A barn owl can place a sound within about 3 degrees side to side and 8 degrees up and down. A phone's microphone cannot tell direction, so this view leaves direction out.
